newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Senate approves zero-based budgeting plan.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Senate approves zero-based budgeting plan.

text.p: California's Senate on Tuesday approved a measure that would overhaul the state's annual budgeting process.
The Senate voted 29-to-4 in favor of Senate Constitutional Amendment 13, sending it to the Assembly for review.
If approved by the Assembly, it would appear on the state ballot.
Last year, the state Assembly and Senate approved a similar measure, but it was vetoed by Gov. Pete Wilson.

This time, Democratic state Senator Jack O'Connell and Republican Senator Tim Leslie introduced their zero-based budgeting proposal as a constitutional amendment that would bypass Wilson, a Republican, and appear on the 1998 ballot.

California's Constitution requires the governor each year to submit to the state legislature a budget itemizing state expenditures and estimating state revenues, and requires the legislature to pass the budget bill by midnight on June 15.
The proposal by O'Connell and Leslie would require so-called zero-based budgeting in putting together the annual blueprint for state spending.
Zero-based budgeting requires state agencies to start with a base of zero dollars, adding funding for programs deemed appropriate.
If approved by state voters, the proposed budgeting reforms would take effect in the 2000-2001 fiscal year.
Supporters of zero-based budgeting argue that the reforms would lead to greater fiscal responsibility and would make it easier to review the governor's annual spending proposals.
"Zero-based budgeting will force state agencies to pause and think seriously about the real need for each program," O'Connell told reporters.
"This isn't a cure-all, but another tool to use to improve the operations of the state for the benefit of taxpayers," O'Connell said.
Wilson's Department of Finance said a similar attempt at zero-based budgeting in the 1970s was a failure, was time-consuming and costly, and did not affect budget decisions.
